pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 10–11 years

- **Topic:** Light Travels in Straight Lines

- **Standards — UK (DfE Year 6 Science, Light):** recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines; use the idea that light travels in straight lines to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them.

- **Standards — US (NGSS):** No elementary performance expectation names rectilinear propagation directly. The Framework develops it implicitly — under 1-PS4-3 the boundary states 'the idea that light travels from place to place is developed through experiences with light sources, mirrors, and shadows, but no attempt is made to discuss the speed of light' — and the geometric light-path model is assessed at 4-PS4-2 ('[curriculum wording omitted; reference 4-PS4-2]'). Explicit ray/straight-line modelling is formalised later at the MS-PS4 band.

- **Operational details:** The leap here is to treat light as something that TRAVELS, along a continuous straight path, through the dark space between source and object — not merely as brightness that exists in lit places. Demonstrate rectilinear travel directly: a narrow torch beam in a darkened, slightly dusty/smoky room; the classic three-holes-in-card line-up (light reaches the eye only when the holes are collinear); a rolled tube proving you cannot see round corners. Teach ray-diagram conventions deliberately — ruler-straight lines, an arrow on every ray showing direction, rays drawn from the source. Then USE straight-line travel to explain shadows: rays graze the edges of an opaque object, so the shadow reproduces the object's outline; children try (and fail) to make light bend round the object. Keep correcting the language trap that 'a ray' is a real thin sliver of light — it is a model of the path's direction.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). At 10–11 this is a transitional abstraction: light is modelled as a continuous straight path through space (including the dark gap), represented by the ray diagram. The threshold is moving from 'light is in the bright bits' to 'light travelled there in a straight line', and then deploying that model to PREDICT and EXPLAIN (shadow shape, why holes must align). Mastery is using straight-line travel as an explanatory tool, not just stating the slogan.
bestPractices: Demonstrate rectilinear travel directly: a narrow torch beam in a darkened (slightly hazy) room; the three-holes-in-card line-up where light only reaches the eye when the holes are collinear; a rolled tube showing you cannot see round corners.
Teach ray-diagram conventions explicitly — ruler-straight lines, a direction arrow on every ray, rays drawn starting from the light source.
Use straight-line travel as an explanatory tool: show rays grazing an opaque object's edges so the shadow reproduces the outline, and have children predict shadow shape from the rays.
Set a 'try to break it' task — ask children to make light bend round a corner or wrap behind the object — so the impossibility makes 'light goes straight' a felt constraint.
Correct the language trap that a 'ray' is a real thin piece of light; frame it as a model of the path and its direction, and that light does not 'add up' from separate rays.
Anchor to the idea that light fills the dark space between source and object as it travels, not only the bright patches where it lands.
keyRepresentations: Ray diagram with ruler-straight, arrowed lines drawn from the source
Three holes in card threaded onto a straight line (often with string) so light reaches the eye only when aligned
A rolled tube held to the eye — 'you can't see round corners'
A torch beam through a slit/smoke showing the straight path
Opaque object on a screen with rays grazing its edges, casting an outline-matching shadow
commonMisconceptions: Light isn't thought of as travelling at all — it simply 'is' wherever it is bright.
Light exists only in the bright regions, not in the space in between as it journeys.
Light bends or curves around edges/corners (so why would shadows be sharp?).
A 'light ray' is a real, physical thin sliver of light rather than a model of the path's direction.
Light is 'made of rays added together'.
Light only travels in straight lines when it comes from a mirror or a laser, not in general.

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: build the idea that light TRAVELS along a continuous straight path through the dark space between a source and an object — not merely that light 'is' wherever it is bright. Learners test rectilinear travel by trying to violate it (holes must align, light won't turn corners), then USE straight-line travel to explain why a shadow reproduces the object's outline. The target is deploying the straight-line model to predict and explain, not reciting the slogan. The ray is taught explicitly as a model of the path and its direction, not a physical sliver of light.

activities.title: Fire a beam, block it, and discover light won't turn corners
feedback: If a learner expects light to still get through an off-line hole, show the alignment failure directly, then connect it: a shadow keeps the object's outline because light does not bend round behind the object either.
If a learner draws only bright patches and no travelling ray, reveal the path with chalk dust or smoke in the beam — the ray IS the path light is taking, present whether or not it has yet landed.
When the 'make light bend' task fails every time, name it: light travels in straight lines, and in this setup, with no mirror or other surface to redirect it, it does not curve round the corner.
activities.rationale: Shadow and image tasks are hard because learners rarely work through what straight-line travel implies; a predict-try-observe cycle that invites learners to attempt to break the rule is intended to turn 'light goes straight' into a felt constraint rather than a stated fact.
sourceClaims: Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.

Year 6 statutory light content: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them; Oak Year 6 teaches ray diagrams, the journey of light, and names the 'a ray is a thin piece of light' / 'light made of rays added together' misconceptions, recommending demonstrations and diagram practice.
learnerActions: Aim a torch across a darkened scene so the beam's straight-edged path becomes visible (use a slightly hazy/dusty or smoky room, where particles scatter some light to your eyes, or draw the beam with straight ray lines, so the travelling path shows).

Place a card with a single hole in the beam's path. Slide the hole until light passes through and reaches a small 'eye' on the far side; note it only gets through when the hole sits on the straight line between torch and eye.
Nudge the hole off that line and observe the light is blocked — it will not bend to find the gap.

Drop an opaque shape into the beam and observe the light passing straight past its edges, throwing a shadow on a screen whose outline matches the shape as seen from the torch (it may be bigger or stretched depending on distances and how the shape and screen are angled).
Try to 'make the shadow wrap round the back of the object' or 'bend the light round the corner' — and find you cannot.
activities.intendedInsight: Light travels in straight lines through the space between source and object; a shadow has the object's outline (as seen from the source) because light travels straight past the edges and does not turn corners into the space behind the object, unless something such as a mirror redirects it.

activities.title: Three holes in a line — predict, then break the alignment
feedback: Expected result: you no longer see the light. Light travels in straight lines, so it passes through all three holes only when they are lined up; it cannot bend to reach the offset middle hole.
If a learner predicts the light still gets through (light 'finds its way' or curves round), run the demo so the failure is seen, then link it to why shadows have the same outline as the object.
If a learner says 'you'd still see it because light is everywhere in the room anyway', revisit the beam-in-dust observation to separate light that has landed from light still travelling.
On the dust question: you are seeing the dust scattering the light into your eye, not light that is simply 'everywhere' — the visible beam marks the straight path the light is travelling along.
activities.rationale: Requiring a straight alignment and then deliberately breaking it, while asking WHY, is intended to force the straight-line mechanism into the open: a 'spreads everywhere / curves to find its way' intuition makes a wrong, testable prediction here.
sourceClaims: Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.
learnerActions: Line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so light passes through all three holes to your eye (threading string through the holes helps show the straight line).
Before moving anything, predict: if you slide the MIDDLE card sideways, will you still see the light? Say why first.
Slide the middle card off-line and check your prediction.
Explain what the result proves about how light travels.
Discuss: when you see the beam in dusty air, are you seeing the light itself or the dust it lights up?
activities.intendedInsight: Light reaches the eye only when the holes are lined up; the offset-hole result contradicts a 'light bends to find its way' model and supports the model that light travels in straight lines.

activities.title: Draw and use ray diagrams to predict a shadow
feedback: Check for the conventions: rays start at the source, are ruler-straight, and carry a direction arrow.

If a learner treats a 'ray' as a real thin sliver of light you could touch, reframe it: a ray is a representation of the direction light travels — a line with an arrow — not a physical strand, and light is not 'made of rays added together'.
If the predicted outline doesn't match, trace the edge-grazing rays together to see where they land on the screen.
activities.rationale: Explicit teaching of ray-diagram conventions, combined with predicting shadow shape before checking, is intended to move learners from stating the rule to using it as an explanatory and predictive tool.
sourceClaims: Year 6 statutory light content: recognise that light appears to travel in straight lines and use this to explain why shadows have the same shape as the objects that cast them; Oak Year 6 teaches ray diagrams, the journey of light, and names the 'a ray is a thin piece of light' / 'light made of rays added together' misconceptions, recommending demonstrations and diagram practice.

Research finds tasks on shadows and images are very difficult because students have rarely thought through what it means for light to travel in a straight line; inquiry-based, prediction-observation curricula effectively build understanding of the implications of light's linear travel for shadows and images.
learnerActions: Draw rays with a ruler as straight lines starting from the light source, putting a direction arrow on every ray.
Draw rays grazing the edges of an opaque object and continuing to a screen to show where the shadow falls and why its outline matches the object.
Predict the shadow's outline for a given shape BEFORE revealing or checking the actual result, then compare.
Explain in words why the shadow reproduces the object's outline, referring to the straight rays past its edges.
activities.intendedInsight: A correct source–object–screen ray diagram with ruler-straight, arrowed rays from the source both represents straight-line travel and lets you predict shadow shape.

activities.title: You can't see round corners
feedback: If a learner expects to see round the bend, have them trace the straight tube with a ruler or string to show the sightline cannot curve.
Connect back: the same straightness is why shadows have the object's outline and why the three holes must align.
activities.rationale: A quick, concrete demonstration gives a memorable everyday anchor for rectilinear travel that complements the beam and ray-diagram work.
learnerActions: Hold a rolled tube to your eye and confirm you can only see what is straight ahead through it.
Try to use the tube to see something off to one side, around a corner — and find you cannot.
Explain how this shows that light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye.
activities.intendedInsight: Because light travels in straight lines from an object to your eye, you cannot see round a corner without something like a mirror to redirect the light.

constraints: Keep correcting the language trap: a 'ray' is a model of the path's direction (a line with an arrow), not a real thin piece of light; and light is not 'made of separate rays added together'.
Emphasise that light fills and travels through the dark space between source and object as it journeys, not only the bright patches where it lands.

This is a transitional/early-formal abstraction for 10–11: mastery is using straight-line travel to predict and explain (shadow shape, hole alignment), not merely stating 'light travels in straight lines'.

Recognition-only checks (e.g. choosing 'straight' vs 'curves' from options) can assess the conclusion but do not require the learner to build the model against the 'light is just in bright places' intuition, so pair them with predict-and-explain tasks.

A labelled, non-manipulable ray diagram is a useful reference for conventions but asserts the straight path rather than letting learners test what happens at a hole or an edge; use it alongside, not instead of, the test-it tasks.

Shadow POSITION and length are genuinely spatial and a three-dimensional sun–object–ground setup can help with those; the specific claim here (shape from straight rays grazing edges) reads cleanly in a flat ray view, so a 3D model is an optional affordance for this sub-concept, not required.

Smoke/dust/haze to reveal the beam needs a suitably darkened space and sensible safety; it is one way to make the travelling path visible, not the only one. Use an ordinary torch rather than a laser or the sun: children may glance briefly through aligned holes to see a modest torch, but should never stare into an intense source and should otherwise keep observations to the beam, the holes, and the cast shadow or a screen.

NGSS note: no elementary performance expectation names rectilinear propagation directly; grade 1 work on light (1-PS4-3, which excludes the speed of light) uses materials placed in a beam and shadows, 4-PS4-2 models light reflecting from objects into the eye, and tracing light's path as straight lines is developed at the middle-school PS4 band.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the three sources are marked verified:false in the row (Oak National Academy unit; Wosilait/Heron/Shaffer/McDermott PER citation); only the NextGenScience boundary claim is marked verified:true. Treat the unverified claims accordingly.

A conversation/dialogue format was judged a poor fit in the source. Reframed as a narrow affordance: narration can convey information but does not itself elicit the hands-on beam manipulation this discovery task relies on; this is a design judgment, not demonstrated evidence that dialogue cannot teach the concept. Retained as context only, not as an activity.

The source's framing that a flat ray view makes 3D 'add cost beyond what this sub-concept needs' is a design preference, not an established efficacy claim; recast as an optional affordance with a stated scope (shape vs. position/length).

The pedagogy lists the misconception 'light only travels straight when it comes from a mirror or a laser, not in general', which is not directly addressed by any activity; consider adding a prompt that general (non-mirror, non-laser) light also travels straight.

No arithmetic or force/motion errors were present to correct; the physics of rectilinear propagation and shadow formation as stated is sound for this level. The main conceptual care point is keeping 'ray' as a model, which is retained in constraints and feedback.

assess.poeTask: Predict whether you will still see the torch through all three holes after the middle card is nudged sideways. Say why first. Then slide the card and explain what the result proves about how light travels.
probeDeeper: Why does a shadow have the same outline shape as the object that casts it?
If light COULD bend round objects, what would shadows look like — could you even have a sharp shadow at all?
When you see a torch beam in dusty air, what are you actually seeing — the light itself, or the dust it lights up?
assess.correctAnswer: No — you no longer see the light. Light travels in straight lines, so it can only pass through all three holes when they are lined up straight; it cannot bend to get through the offset middle hole.

errorPatterns.pattern: Light bends round corners: 'the light curves round the edge to get where it needs to go' — the tell is 'I can see light near a corner so it must bend'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do the align-the-holes demo so the failure is seen; then connect it to shadows — a shadow has the object's sharp outline precisely because light cannot bend round the object.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — light bends around inside to get through the middle hole.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Predicts light still passes the offset hole; says light 'finds its way' or bends round the card

errorPatterns.pattern: Light is only in bright patches: light exists where it lands, not travelling through the space between torch and wall (no ray in the air between)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Reveal the travelling path with chalk dust or smoke in the beam — the ray IS the path light takes; it is there whether or not it has landed yet.
errorPatterns.distractor: You'd still see it, because the light is everywhere in the room anyway.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Draws bright spots but no travelling ray; denies light is 'in' the air between source and object

errorPatterns.pattern: Ray as a physical object: 'a ray is a thin solid piece of light you could touch'
errorPatterns.nextMove: A ray is a representation of the DIRECTION light travels, drawn as a line with an arrow — not a physical strand of light.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Talks about a ray as a thing/object rather than as the path or direction light travels

responseLevels.gap: Predicts light still passes the offset hole / says light bends round corners, or denies light travels through the space between the source and the wall.
responseLevels.full: Predicts the offset hole blocks the light AND explains it by straight-line travel; transfers the idea to shadow shape and draws a correct source-object-screen ray diagram.
responseLevels.partial: States that light travels in straight lines but cannot use it — e.g. cannot explain the offset-hole result, or why a shadow matches the object's outline.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: You line up three cards, each with a small hole punched in the middle, and shine a torch so you can see the light through all three holes. Now you slide the MIDDLE card sideways a little. Will you still see the light coming through? Explain what this tells you about how light travels.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who thinks light 'spreads everywhere' or 'curves to find its way' predicts you'd still see it through the offset hole. Requiring a straight alignment and then breaking it, while asking WHY, forces the straight-line mechanism: the offset-hole result simply cannot be explained by a light-bends-round model.
